title: The brainstem: crossed signs and the rule of four
description: How a crossed pattern of signs places a lesion in the brainstem, how the rule of four turns that anatomy into arithmetic, and what changes when the lesion is a child's tumor.
why: Crossed signs are how the brainstem announces itself, and the rule of four turns its maze of nuclei and tracts into something close to arithmetic.
objectives: Recognize a crossed pattern and use the cranial nerve to name the side and the level.
Apply the rule of four to predict the findings of a medial or lateral lesion at each level, and name its exceptions.
Decode the classic brainstem syndromes as combinations of structures.
Use eye movements and nystagmus to separate hemispheric, brainstem and peripheral causes, and judge a child's sixth-nerve palsy by its company.

sections.title: Why crossed findings mean the brainstem
sections.content:
Most lesions in the nervous system keep their effects on one side of the body. A stroke in the internal capsule weakens the opposite face, arm and leg together, and a lesion of the spinal cord leaves the face alone entirely. The brainstem breaks this habit, and the way it breaks it is what identifies it. The cranial nerve nuclei there sit beside long tracts that have not yet finished their journey. The corticospinal tract in particular crosses only at the bottom of the medulla, so through most of the brainstem it still serves the **opposite** body. A single small lesion can therefore catch a cranial nerve on its **own side** and the limbs on the **other**, a pattern called an alternating hemiplegia. Crossed signs, with a cranial nerve affected on one side and the body on the other, point to the brainstem (Brazis 2011, p. 12).

**Two facts in one sign**

A crossed pattern answers two questions at once. The cranial nerve finding gives you the **side**, because a cranial nerve nucleus or fascicle serves its own side of the head. Its **number** gives you the **level**, because the nuclei are stacked in order, with the third at the midbrain, the sixth and seventh in the pons and the twelfth in the medulla. The limb signs then tell you how far toward the front or the middle the lesion reaches. Facial sensation follows the same logic. A brainstem lesion numbs pinprick on the face of its own side, because the descending trigeminal tract has not yet crossed, and it often numbs the body on the other side as well (Pearl 2014, p. 47).

**At the bedside**

When a weak arm and leg arrive together with a cranial nerve finding, the first thing to settle is which side the cranial nerve is on. If the face and limbs are weak on the same side, the lesion lies above the facial nucleus, usually in the hemisphere, though the cerebral peduncle or upper pons can do the same (Brazis 2011, p. 11). If they are on opposite sides, the lesion is in the brainstem, and the cranial nerve tells you the level. The [[m01-where-before-what|first module]] argued that the most useful findings are the ones that exclude levels. A crossed pattern excludes every level except the brainstem, provided the findings began together.

The reasoning is the same in children, but the causes differ. Tumors, demyelination and inflammation are more common in children than the vascular syndromes that fill adult textbooks.
keyPoints: Crossed signs, with a cranial nerve affected on one side and the limbs on the other, point to the brainstem (Brazis 2011, p. 12).
The cranial nerve finding lies on the side of the lesion, and the number of the nerve gives the level.
The corticospinal tract crosses only at the bottom of the medulla, so above that point it still serves the opposite body.
When the face and limbs are weak on the same side, the lesion lies above the facial nucleus rather than in the lower brainstem.

question.question: A 9-year-old has weakness of the whole left side of the face, including the forehead, and a weak right arm and leg with a brisk right knee jerk. Where is the lesion?
options: The right internal capsule
The right cerebral cortex
The left pons
The cervical spinal cord on the left
question.explanation: Because the forehead is involved, the facial weakness is of lower motor neuron type and comes from the facial nucleus or its fascicle on the left. The weak right limbs with a brisk reflex are upper motor neuron and on the opposite side. A cranial nerve on one side with the limbs on the other is a crossed pattern, and since the seventh nerve lives in the pons, a lesion in the left pons explains every finding. A lesion of the right internal capsule or the right cortex would weaken the left face and the left limbs together and would spare the forehead. The spinal cord contains no cranial nerves, so a cord lesion cannot account for the facial palsy at all.

sections.title: The rule of four
sections.content:
The brainstem can look like a maze of nuclei and tracts with nineteenth-century names. The rule of four turns the maze into something close to arithmetic, and it is worth learning precisely because it simplifies ([Gates 2005](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15836511/); [Gates 2011](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21551111/)). It asks you to remember a few groups of four, which the rest of this section lays out.

**Four medial structures, all beginning with M**

- **M**otor pathway, the corticospinal tract, whose damage weakens the **opposite** arm and leg.
- **M**edial lemniscus, which carries vibration and position sense from the **opposite** body.
- **M**edial longitudinal fasciculus, whose damage gives an internuclear ophthalmoplegia on the **same** side.
- **M**otor nucleus and nerve, meaning the cranial nerves whose numbers divide evenly into 12 (3, 4, 6 and 12), affected on the **same** side.

**Four lateral structures, all beginning with S**

- **S**pinocerebellar pathways, giving ataxia of the **same** arm and leg.
- **S**pinothalamic tract, with pain and temperature lost on the **opposite** body.
- **S**ensory nucleus of the fifth nerve, with pain and temperature lost on the **same** side of the face.
- **S**ympathetic pathway, with a Horner syndrome on the **same** side.

**Four cranial nerves at each level**

The medulla holds 9 to 12 and the pons 5 to 8, and the four above the pons are 1 to 4, of which 3 and 4 sit in the midbrain. The motor nuclei whose numbers do not divide evenly into 12 (5, 7, 9 and 11) lie laterally, and so do the eighth nerve in the pons and the tenth in the medulla. A medial lesion therefore names its level by 3, 6 or 12. A lateral lesion names it by 5, 7 and 8 in the pons, or by 9 and 10 in the medulla. The figure above lets you place a lesion at each level, medial and lateral, and watch the findings assemble themselves.

**Where the rule bends**

A heuristic is most useful when you know where it fails, and this one bends in four places. The fourth nerve has a medial midbrain nucleus, but its fibers cross before they leave, so a nuclear lesion weakens the **opposite** superior oblique. The facial fascicle runs medially and loops around the sixth nucleus, so a medial pontine lesion often takes the face with it. The rule places the eighth nerve in the pons, but the vestibular nuclei reach down into the lateral medulla, so a lateral medullary lesion usually brings vertigo and nystagmus. The rule also places the eleventh nerve in the lateral medulla, yet a lateral medullary stroke rarely weakens the shoulder shrug. Real lesions, especially tumors in children, also ignore a tidy line between medial and lateral. The rule is best used to decide what to look for, and the examination then shows what is actually there.
keyPoints: The four medial structures are the motor pathway, the medial lemniscus, the medial longitudinal fasciculus and the motor cranial nerves 3, 4, 6 and 12.

The four lateral structures are the spinocerebellar pathways, the spinothalamic tract, the sensory nucleus of 5 and the sympathetic pathway. The lateral cranial nerves are 5, 7 and 8 in the pons and 9, 10 and 11 in the medulla, though 11 is rarely affected in practice.
Long-tract signs from the motor pathway, the lemniscus and the spinothalamic tract appear on the opposite side, and everything else appears on the side of the lesion.
The rule is a heuristic (Gates 2005), and it bends where the fourth nerve crosses, where the facial fascicle strays medially and where lateral medullary lesions bring vertigo.

question.question: A teenager has a right-sided lesion in the lateral pons. Using the rule of four, which combination do you expect?
options: Right facial weakness and numbness with right ataxia and Horner syndrome, plus loss of pain and temperature on the left body
Right sixth-nerve palsy with left hemiparesis and left loss of position sense
Left facial numbness, left Horner syndrome and right body numbness
Right third-nerve palsy with left hemiparesis
question.explanation: A lateral pontine lesion takes the cranial nerves that sit laterally in the pons (5, 7 and 8) together with the four lateral S structures. Every resulting sign appears on the side of the lesion except the loss of pain and temperature on the body, which is on the opposite side. A sixth-nerve palsy with opposite hemiparesis and lost position sense is the medial pontine pattern and belongs to a different lesion. Placing the facial signs and the Horner syndrome on the left reverses the sides, since those structures are uncrossed at this level. A third-nerve palsy with opposite hemiparesis comes from the medial midbrain.

sections.title: Named syndromes as worked examples
sections.content:
Eponyms have a bad reputation, and some of it is deserved. A name records who described a patient and tells you nothing about where the lesion is. Each classic brainstem syndrome, however, is also a worked example of the rule of four. Decoding them is good practice if you read each one as a lesion with a level and a side, as in the table below (Pearl 2014, pp. 109-112; Brazis 2011, pp. 393, 397).

| Syndrome | Where | Same side | Opposite side |
|---|---|---|---|
| Weber | Ventral midbrain, cerebral peduncle | Third-nerve palsy, with a dilated pupil | Hemiparesis including the lower face |
| Benedikt | Midbrain tegmentum through the red nucleus | Third-nerve palsy | Hemiparesis, with tremor and ataxia |
| Millard-Gubler | Ventral pons | Sixth- and seventh-nerve palsies | Hemiparesis |
| Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) | Lateral medulla | Face numb to pin, ataxia, Horner syndrome, hoarseness and difficulty swallowing, vertigo and nystagmus | Body numb to pain and temperature |
| Medial medullary (Dejerine) | Medial medulla | Tongue weakness | Hemiparesis and loss of position sense |

**Decoding Weber and Benedikt**

Weber syndrome is the medial midbrain in its simplest form, with the third-nerve fascicle and the corticospinal tract lying side by side in the peduncle. The third-nerve palsy includes the pupil, because the parasympathetic fibers travel with the nerve (Brazis 2011, p. 397). A lesion further back, in the tegmentum, also takes in the red nucleus. The cerebellar outflow passes through the red nucleus on its way to the thalamus, so the opposite limbs now shake as well (Pearl 2014, p. 110).

**Decoding Wallenberg**

The lateral medulla is the purest test of the S structures, and the lateral medullary syndrome contains every one of them. The spinal trigeminal tract accounts for numbness of the face on the same side, and the syndrome adds ataxia and a Horner syndrome on that side, with numbness of the body on the opposite side. The nucleus ambiguus brings hoarseness and a poor swallow, and the vestibular nuclei bring vertigo, nausea and vomiting. The syndrome causes no weakness, because the corticospinal tract runs medially and a purely lateral lesion misses it (Pearl 2014, p. 111).

**Why it matters for children**

Classic vascular syndromes are uncommon in childhood, but the skill of decoding them is needed all the time. A child with a pontine tumor or a demyelinating plaque rarely matches a whole row of the table and more often shows part of one. Knowing the full pattern lets you recognize the part and predict which neighboring signs to look for next.
keyPoints: An eponym is best read as a lesion, by asking which structures it involves, on which side and at which level.
Weber syndrome is the medial midbrain, with a same-side third-nerve palsy that includes the pupil and an opposite hemiparesis (Brazis 2011, p. 397).
Wallenberg syndrome is the lateral medulla, with same-side facial numbness, ataxia, Horner syndrome, vertigo and nystagmus, opposite body numbness, and no weakness.
The medial medullary syndrome gives same-side tongue weakness with opposite hemiparesis and loss of position sense (Pearl 2014, p. 112).

question.question: A 16-year-old develops vertigo and vomiting, a hoarse voice, numbness to pin on the left face and right body, a small left pupil with slight ptosis, and clumsiness of the left arm. Strength is normal. Where is the lesion, and which finding most argues against it being medial?
options: Right lateral pons; the vertigo argues against medial
Left medial medulla; the hoarse voice argues against lateral
Left midbrain tegmentum; the Horner syndrome argues against medial
Left lateral medulla; normal strength argues against medial
question.explanation: Numbness of the face, a Horner syndrome and ataxia on the same side, numbness of the body on the opposite side, and hoarseness from the nucleus ambiguus together make the lateral medullary syndrome, here on the left. Normal strength is the clue that the lesion is lateral, because the corticospinal tract runs medially and a medial lesion would have caught it. A right lateral pontine lesion would put the facial and Horner signs on the right. A medial medullary lesion would weaken the tongue and the opposite limbs, which this teenager does not have. The hoarse voice cannot come from the midbrain, which contains no ninth or tenth nerve.

sections.title: The eyes as a brainstem map
sections.content:
The circuits that move the eyes run from the frontal eye fields down the whole length of the brainstem to the vestibular nuclei at the pontomedullary junction. That makes eye movements one of the most sensitive tests of the brainstem you have. Three eye findings in particular are worth knowing well enough to recognize at a glance.

**Internuclear ophthalmoplegia**

The medial longitudinal fasciculus links the sixth nucleus on one side to the third nucleus on the other, so that both eyes turn together. When it is cut and the patient looks away from the lesion, the eye on the side of the lesion fails to adduct while the abducting eye jerks with nystagmus (Pearl 2014, p. 45). The fasciculus is one of the four medial structures in the rule of four. It localizes precisely, because the eye that fails to adduct is on the side of the lesion.

**Which way the eyes look**

A destructive lesion of one frontal eye field leaves the other unopposed, so the eyes deviate **toward** a hemispheric lesion and away from the hemiparesis. A pontine lesion destroys the horizontal gaze center beside the sixth nucleus, so the eyes deviate **away** from the lesion and toward the hemiparesis (Pearl 2014, pp. 43, 148). A seizure reverses the hemispheric rule by exciting the eye field, which drives the eyes away from the focus (Pearl 2014, p. 9). The doll's-eye maneuver separates a hemispheric cause from a pontine one. It can overcome a cortical gaze preference, but it cannot overcome a pontine gaze palsy, because the gaze center itself is gone (Pearl 2014, p. 45).

**Central or peripheral nystagmus**

A few bedside rules separate the two (Pearl 2014, pp. 120-121).

- Peripheral (labyrinth) nystagmus beats in one direction, is suppressed when the patient fixates, and often has a torsional part.
- Nystagmus that changes direction with gaze is central.
- Pure vertical nystagmus is central.
- Acquired pendular nystagmus is usually central.
- Central nystagmus keeps company with other brainstem or cerebellar signs ("everything in neurology is based on the company you keep", Pearl 2014, p. 121).

Antiseizure drugs can also produce a nystagmus that looks central (Pearl 2014, p. 121), which matters in children being treated for epilepsy.

**In a child**

Children rarely complain of double vision. More often they close one eye, tilt the head or turn the face, so watch the head posture before you test the eyes, and test pursuit with a toy rather than a finger.
keyPoints: In internuclear ophthalmoplegia the eye on the side of the lesion fails to adduct, and the other eye shows abducting nystagmus (Pearl 2014, p. 45).
The eyes look toward a destructive hemispheric lesion and away from a pontine one (Pearl 2014, pp. 43, 148), while a seizure drives them away from the focus.
The doll's-eye maneuver overcomes a cortical gaze preference but cannot overcome a pontine gaze palsy.
Nystagmus that changes direction, is purely vertical or resists fixation is central, and the company it keeps should always be checked.

question.question: A 12-year-old with a left hemiparesis has both eyes deviated to the right. On a doll's-eye maneuver the eyes move fully to the left. Where is the lesion?
options: The left pons
The right hemisphere
The left frontal lobe, during a seizure
The right medial longitudinal fasciculus
question.explanation: Eyes deviated to the right with a left hemiparesis are looking toward the lesion and away from the weak side, which is the pattern of a destructive right hemispheric lesion. The doll's-eye maneuver confirms it, because a cortical gaze preference can be overcome when the brainstem gaze center is intact. A left pontine lesion would also push the eyes to the right, but its gaze palsy could not be overcome with doll's eyes, and the hemiparesis would be on the right. A left frontal seizure drives the eyes to the right too, yet it explains a fixed left hemiparesis with full doll's eyes far less well than a destructive right lesion does. An internuclear ophthalmoplegia causes failure of adduction in one eye rather than a conjugate deviation of both.

sections.title: Inside the nerve
sections.content:
Most of this module asks where a lesion sits along the length of the brainstem. For the third nerve it is worth asking a narrower question, which is where the lesion sits **inside** the nerve, because the answer predicts the mechanism.

**Who rides on the outside**

The parasympathetic fibers that constrict the pupil are wrapped around the surface of the third nerve, while the fibers to the eye muscles and the lid run through its core (Pearl 2014, pp. 35-36). The small vessels that supply the nerve enter from its surface and feed it from the outside in, so the core is the part that starves first (Pearl 2014, p. 38). Compression and ischemia therefore damage different fibers.

- **Compression** presses on the surface, so the pupil fibers fail early and the pupil dilates (Pearl 2014, p. 36).
- **Ischemia** starves the core, giving ptosis and an eye that will not adduct, with a normal pupil (Pearl 2014, p. 38; Brazis 2011, p. 190).

The rule has exceptions, since a compressive lesion occasionally spares the pupil, an ischemic one sometimes involves it a little, and an incomplete palsy with a normal pupil can still hide a mass (Brazis 2011, p. 190). The pupil shifts the odds without settling the question.

**What changes in a child**

Adult teaching relies on two examples, the aneurysm that compresses and the diabetic nerve that starves (Pearl 2014, pp. 35, 38). Microvascular ischemia is rare in children, so a child with an acquired third-nerve palsy usually needs imaging even when the pupil is normal. Children also bring a different set of causes, and three of them are worth knowing.

- **Congenital palsy**, which is rare, usually unilateral and sometimes accompanied by other cranial nerve or brain malformations. The pupil is usually involved but is more often **small** than large, probably from aberrant regeneration (Brazis 2011, p. 192), which is another exception to the pupil rule.
- **Ophthalmoplegic migraine** (now classified as recurrent painful ophthalmoplegic neuropathy), a reversible cause (Pearl 2014, p. 38) that usually begins in the first decade (Brazis 2011, p. 192).
- **Trauma**, and infection or inflammation of the meninges along the nerve's course (Brazis 2011, p. 191).

**The pupil that tells the side**

The same anatomy explains what happens to the pupil in uncal herniation. A swelling temporal lobe stretches the third nerve, and the pupil dilates first, before the eye movements fail (Brazis 2011, p. 191). The hemiparesis may be on the wrong side, but the dilated pupil reliably marks the side of the mass (Pearl 2014, p. 37). [[m10-everywhere|Module 10]] returns to this sign when it follows the herniating brain downward.

> **Bedside trick.** Myasthenia can imitate a pupil-sparing third-nerve palsy, so it belongs on the list whenever ptosis or double vision is painless and the pupil is normal. Ask the child to hold an upward gaze, because myasthenic ptosis deepens with the effort. Then watch the lid as the eyes come back from looking down, since it may briefly twitch upward (Brazis 2011, p. 181).
keyPoints: Pupil fibers ride on the outside of the third nerve, and the blood supply feeds the nerve from the outside in (Pearl 2014, pp. 35-38).
Compression dilates the pupil early and ischemia of the core spares it, though this is a probability that has exceptions (Brazis 2011, p. 190).
In children, think of congenital palsy (in which the pupil is often small), ophthalmoplegic migraine and trauma (Brazis 2011, pp. 191-192; Pearl 2014, p. 38).
In uncal herniation the dilated pupil marks the side of the mass more reliably than the hemiparesis does (Pearl 2014, p. 37).
Painless ptosis or double vision with a normal pupil should raise the possibility of myasthenia (Brazis 2011, p. 181).

question.question: A 12-year-old has two weeks of worsening headache. His left lid droops, the left eye cannot adduct or look up, and the left pupil is larger than the right and reacts sluggishly. What does the pupil add to your reasoning?
options: Nothing, because the pupil does not help separate the causes of a third-nerve palsy
It favors ischemia of the core of the nerve, so the child can be observed
It suggests something pressing on the surface of the nerve, so the brain should be imaged urgently
It points to myasthenia, which commonly enlarges the pupil
question.explanation: The pupil fibers travel on the outside of the third nerve, so a dilated, sluggish pupil with the palsy suggests compression from outside, and together with a worsening headache that calls for urgent imaging (Pearl 2014, pp. 35-36). Ischemia tempts anyone trained on adult diabetic palsies, but it is rare in children, and it starves the core of the nerve and typically spares the pupil (Pearl 2014, p. 38). Myasthenia mimics a pupil-sparing palsy precisely because it leaves the pupil alone (Brazis 2011, p. 181). Far from being neutral, the pupil is the most useful single sign in this child.

sections.title: The child's brainstem
sections.content:
Brainstem localization in adults is taught through strokes. In children it is taught through tumors, malformations and inflammation, so the logic has to cope with lesions that grow, infiltrate and compress without respecting any arterial territory.

**The posterior fossa**

Primary posterior fossa tumors are common in children, and two of the commonest are medulloblastoma and the cystic cerebellar astrocytoma (Pearl 2014, p. 63). Medulloblastoma accounts for about 20% of pediatric brain tumors. It tends to begin in the caudal vermis, giving a staggering gait and truncal imbalance with little limb ataxia at first (Brazis 2011, p. 412). As it grows it blocks the fourth ventricle, and the presenting picture becomes one of raised intracranial pressure, with morning headache, vomiting and papilledema.

**A new sixth-nerve palsy**

The sixth nerve takes a long course across the base of the skull, which leaves it vulnerable to raised pressure anywhere, above or below the tentorium. An abducens palsy can therefore be an early sign of a tumor, hydrocephalus or idiopathic intracranial hypertension rather than of a lesion in the nerve itself (Pearl 2014, p. 43). This is the classic false localizing sign. The rule of four helps you decide whether to believe it, by asking what keeps the palsy company.

- **Papilledema and nothing else** suggests raised pressure, and the palsy then says nothing about where the cause lies.
- **A facial palsy on the same side, a gaze palsy, ataxia or long-tract signs** suggest a lesion in the pons itself, because a single lesion there would catch the sixth nucleus, the facial fascicle that loops around it and the tracts beside them.

**Infiltrating pontine tumors and the Chiari malformation**

A tumor that infiltrates the pons does not stay medial or lateral. It gathers cranial nerves and long tracts as it grows, which is exactly the accumulation the rule of four predicts. In a Chiari malformation the cerebellar tonsils descend through the foramen magnum and crowd the lower brainstem, and a syrinx may form in the cord below. Look for lower cranial nerve signs and for the cape of lost pain sensation described in the [[m06-spinal-cord|spinal cord module]].

**What to examine**

When a child presents with any brainstem sign, the examination should cover the optic discs, every cranial nerve including the palate and tongue, the gait and tandem walk, and the reflexes and plantar responses on both sides. Those findings together then help you decide how urgent the scan needs to be.
keyPoints: Posterior fossa tumors are common in children, and two of the commonest are medulloblastoma and the cystic cerebellar astrocytoma (Pearl 2014, p. 63).
A sixth-nerve palsy can be a false localizing sign of raised intracranial pressure (Pearl 2014, p. 43).
A sixth-nerve palsy is judged by its company, since papilledema alone suggests pressure, while a facial palsy, gaze palsy or long-tract signs suggest the pons.
Infiltrating pontine tumors gather cranial nerves and long tracts as they grow, as the rule of four predicts.

question.question: A 6-year-old has two weeks of morning headaches and vomiting and now turns her face to the right to read. She has a right sixth-nerve palsy and papilledema. Facial movement, strength, reflexes and gait are normal. What is the best interpretation?
options: A lesion in the right pontine tegmentum
Raised intracranial pressure, with the sixth-nerve palsy as a false localizing sign, calling for urgent brain imaging
A benign isolated sixth-nerve palsy after a viral illness; review in a month
A right medial longitudinal fasciculus lesion
question.explanation: Headache, vomiting and papilledema indicate raised intracranial pressure, and the sixth nerve is the cranial nerve most vulnerable to it because of its long course. With no facial palsy, gaze palsy, ataxia or long-tract signs keeping it company, the palsy is best read as a sign of the pressure, and the cause needs urgent imaging. A lesion in the pontine tegmentum would usually bring the facial fascicle or the gaze center with it. Calling the palsy benign ignores the papilledema. A lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus causes failure of adduction, whereas this child cannot abduct.

quiz.question: A 14-year-old has a right lower motor neuron facial palsy, cannot abduct the right eye, and has a left hemiparesis. Where is the lesion?
options: Left internal capsule
Right ventral pons
Right lateral medulla
Left ventral midbrain
quiz.explanation: A sixth- and seventh-nerve palsy on one side with hemiparesis on the other is the ventral pontine (Millard-Gubler) pattern. It comes from damage to the corticospinal tract in the basis pontis and to the sixth and seventh fascicles as they pass nearby (Brazis 2011, p. 393). The rule of four classes the seventh nerve as lateral, so this is one of the rule's known exceptions. A left capsular lesion would weaken the right limbs and spare the forehead. A lateral medullary lesion causes no weakness and involves nerves 9 and 10 rather than 6 and 7. A midbrain lesion would give a third-nerve palsy.

quiz.question: On protrusion the tongue deviates to the left. The right arm and leg are weak, and vibration and position sense are lost in the right limbs. Pain sensation and the face are normal. Where is the lesion?
options: Right medial medulla
Left lateral medulla
Left internal capsule
Left medial medulla
quiz.explanation: The tongue deviates toward the weak side, so the left hypoglossal nucleus or nerve is involved. The right hemiparesis and the loss of vibration and position sense in the right limbs come from the corticospinal tract and the medial lemniscus, both of which are medial and both of which serve the opposite body. The twelfth nerve, the motor pathway and the lemniscus together make the medial medullary (Dejerine) syndrome, here on the left. A right medial medullary lesion would push the tongue to the right. A lateral medullary lesion spares strength. A capsular lesion cannot weaken the tongue on one side and the limbs on the other in this way.

quiz.question: On looking to the left, a teenager's right eye does not cross the midline while the left eye abducts with nystagmus. Convergence is normal. Which structure is damaged?
options: The left sixth-nerve nucleus
The right third nerve
The left frontal eye field
The right medial longitudinal fasciculus
quiz.explanation: Failure of the right eye to adduct on leftward gaze, with abducting nystagmus in the left eye, is a right internuclear ophthalmoplegia, because the right medial longitudinal fasciculus carries the signal from the left sixth nucleus up to the right third nucleus. Normal convergence shows that the third nerve itself works, which excludes a right third-nerve palsy. A lesion of the left sixth nucleus would abolish leftward gaze in both eyes. A frontal eye field lesion causes a conjugate gaze preference rather than the failure of one eye alone.

quiz.question: A 10-year-old has a left third-nerve palsy with a dilated pupil, a right hemiparesis, and a coarse tremor of the right hand that worsens as it reaches for a target. Which structure, beyond those of Weber syndrome, explains the tremor?
options: The red nucleus and the cerebellar outflow passing through it
The left medial lemniscus
The right cerebellar hemisphere
The left substantia nigra
quiz.explanation: A third-nerve palsy with opposite hemiparesis places the lesion in the midbrain. The added tremor and ataxia on the opposite side mean the lesion has reached the tegmentum, where the cerebellar outflow passes through the red nucleus after crossing, and the combination is Benedikt syndrome (Pearl 2014, p. 110). The medial lemniscus carries sensation and would not cause a tremor. A right cerebellar lesion could cause right-sided ataxia but could not explain a left third-nerve palsy. A nigral lesion causes slowness and a tremor at rest, which is a different picture from an action tremor with ataxia.

quiz.question: Which nystagmus in a dizzy 13-year-old should most change your plan from reassurance to an urgent brain MRI?
options: Horizontal-torsional nystagmus beating to the left that settles when she fixes on a target
A few beats of nystagmus at the extreme of lateral gaze
Pure downbeating nystagmus in primary gaze
Nystagmus that appears a few seconds after a positional maneuver and then fatigues
quiz.explanation: Pure vertical nystagmus is central and should send you looking for a lesion in the brainstem or cerebellum. Unidirectional horizontal-torsional nystagmus that is suppressed by fixation is the peripheral pattern. A few beats at the extreme of gaze are physiological end-point nystagmus. Delayed nystagmus that fatigues after a positional maneuver is the peripheral positional pattern (Pearl 2014, pp. 120-121). Because some antiseizure drugs cause a nystagmus that looks central, the medication list also belongs in the history.

quiz.question: A lesion destroys the left trochlear nucleus in the midbrain. Which superior oblique is weak, and why does this matter for the rule of four?
options: The left, because all medial motor nuclei serve their own side
Neither, because the fourth nerve is purely sensory
Both, because the trochlear nuclei are fused in the midline
The right, because the fourth-nerve fibers cross before they exit, which makes it one of the rule's exceptions
quiz.explanation: The trochlear nerve is the only cranial nerve whose fibers cross completely before leaving the brainstem, and it leaves from the back. A nuclear lesion therefore weakens the opposite superior oblique, which breaks the rule that motor cranial nerve findings sit on the side of the lesion, and assuming same-side weakness is exactly the error the rule would lead you into. The fourth nerve is a motor nerve, and its nuclei are paired rather than fused in the midline.

quiz.question: A 3-week-old has had a droopy left eyelid since birth. The left eye rests down and out and moves poorly up and in, and the left pupil is smaller than the right and barely reacts to light. How do you read this?
options: A congenital third-nerve palsy, in which the pupil is often small rather than large
A left Horner syndrome, because the pupil is small
An ischemic third-nerve palsy, because the pupil is not dilated
Myasthenia, because the pupil is abnormal
quiz.explanation: Ptosis with the eye resting down and out and poor elevation and adduction is a third-nerve palsy. In the congenital form the pupil is usually involved but is more often small than dilated, probably from aberrant regeneration (Brazis 2011, p. 192), so the adult rule that a large pupil means compression does not carry over. Horner syndrome tempts because of the small pupil, but it gives a mild ptosis with miosis (Brazis 2011, p. 275) and does not paralyze the eye muscles. Ischemic palsy belongs to adult vascular disease and spares the pupil rather than shrinking it. Myasthenia spares the pupil (Brazis 2011, p. 181).

opener.parable: In the brainstem the long pathways to and from the limbs run right alongside the nuclei of the cranial nerves, so a lesion there almost never affects just one thing. The particular combination of signs is what gives its location away.
opener.history: Many brainstem syndromes carry the names of the physicians who described them between 1858 and 1914. Millard and Gubler came first in 1858, followed by Weber in 1863, Benedikt in 1872, Wallenberg in 1895 and Dejerine in 1914. Each name marks a spot where a cranial nerve and a long tract run close together.
